newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: France says Daewoo should bid again for Thomson.
newsitem.headline: France says Daewoo should bid again for Thomson.

text.p: A day after South Korean President Kim Young-sam lashed out at France over a snub to Daewoo Electronics, a French envoy on Wednesday urged the company to try again to buy Thomson Multimedia.
Jean-Claude Paye also acknowledged that the bungled deal had hurt and humiliated South Korea.
"The French government is hopeful that Daewoo will re-enter a bid," he told a news conference.

Paye, a former head of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, was sent to Seoul as a presidential envoy to repair damage caused by the decision to scuttle the Thomson sale to Daewoo.

"Since Daewoo already once made a near-successful bid, we are sure that it would be looked upon with sympathy, but of course without preference, because the process must be transparent and without prejudice," he said.
State-owned Thomson SA had been slated to be sold to Lagardere Group for a symbolic one franc. Lagardere then planned to sell the Thomson multimedia division to Daewoo for the same sum.
Many South Koreans regard the rejection of Daewoo's bid as an act of overt racism.
President Kim on Tuesday blasted France. A presidential statement said he told Paye: "The South Korean people believe we have been totally discriminated against.
"We have a bad impression of France and have come to think France cannot be trusted," Kim added.
But Paye denied Kim had called France untrustworthy.
"During our meeting, the president did not tell me that France was not a trustworthy nation. He did, however, express his disappointment and confusion over the decision," Paye said.
"The French government recognises the recent events were humiliating and hurtful to the Korean government, the Korean people and the Korean workers."
Paye said France would reopen the privatisation process after the European Commission decided on a planned recapitalisation of ailing Thomson SA.
Paris has requested clearance for its plan to inject 11 billion francs ($2.06 billion) into the group.

Paye said while it was theoretically possible Thomson's privatisation could be cancelled "it is quite clear that the government does not want to retain the assets of this company in the public sector."
Daewoo would now be able to make its case directly to the independent privatisation committee, which earlier ruled out a sale to Daewoo citing concerns over technology transfer.

"During the second round, Daewoo will be able to directly deal with the committee because Thomson Multimedia will be sold off separately," he said. Defense electronics firm Thomson-CSF would be handled differently.
This would avoid confusion about Daewoo's ability to take over the firm that may have coloured the committee's original decision, Paye said.
Daewoo promised to create 5,000 new jobs in France after taking over Thomson Multimedia and its huge debts.

Paye said France would return to South Korea historical documents now in French museums in exchange for other cultural artifacts, an issue that has added fuel to anti-French sentiment following the Thomson sale fiasco.
Details of the exchange had not been worked out, he said.
($1 = 5.35 francs)
